repos.title: SkillOpt: Executive Strategy for Self-Evolving Agent Skills
repos.paper_summary: SkillOpt is a text-space optimizer that trains one agent skill document, a natural-language procedure added to the context of a frozen target model. A separate frontier optimizer model reads scored rollouts from a training split and proposes add, delete, or replace edits. A candidate skill is kept only if it raises the score on a held-out selection split. Stability controls include a cap on edits per step (the "textual learning rate"), a buffer of rejected edits passed to later reflection calls, and an epoch-wise slow/meta update. The paper reports results on six benchmarks, seven target models, and three execution modes (direct chat, Codex, Claude Code). For GPT–5.5 in direct chat, the average gain over no skill is +23.5 points, and the average margin over the strongest per-cell baseline is +5.4 points. Exported skills are 300–2,000 tokens, built from 11–44 accepted edits. The paper also reports transfer across model scales and harnesses, and to Omni-MATH. Limitations: the method optimizes one skill for one domain, and it depends on a separate frontier optimizer model. The provided text ends before the slow/meta update is described, so that component and its ablation results are not covered here.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: SkillOpt optimizes an agent's skill document as external state, with validation-gated edits and no weight updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior skill work mainly builds or evolves skill libraries, while prompt optimizers target prompts rather than a persistent skill.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each step edits the skill with bounded add, delete and replace operations, accepted only if held-out selection score strictly improves.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: SkillOpt is best or tied on all 52 evaluated cells, lifting GPT–5.5 by 23.5 points in direct chat.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Compact skills optimized this way transfer across model scales, harnesses and a nearby benchmark without weight updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists the optimizer prompt contracts, limitations, and experimental protocol with patch and split details.

repos.title: LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation
repos.paper_summary:
LightRAG is a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation system. An LLM extracts entities and relations from chunks of size 1200, profiles each as a key-value pair, and deduplicates the resulting graph. At query time, local keywords match entities and global keywords match relations, and one-hop neighbors of the matches are added as context for a general LLM. New documents are indexed by merging their subgraphs into the existing graph instead of rebuilding it.

The evaluation uses four UltraDomain datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, Mix), with 125 generated questions per dataset, GPT-4o-mini as the default LLM, and pairwise LLM judgments reported as win rates. Against NaiveRAG on Legal, LightRAG wins 84.8% overall. Against GraphRAG, the margins are small: overall win rates of 54.8% on Agriculture, 52.0% on CS, 52.8% on Legal, and 49.6% on Mix.

The judgments come from a single LLM judge, not human or ground-truth labels. The ablation and cost results are cut off in the provided text, so this summary does not report them.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems rely on flat representations and produce fragmented answers, so the paper proposes graph-based indexing with incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
digest_headlines.headline: The paper formalizes RAG as indexing and retrieval followed by generation, and sets three design goals for an efficient system.

digest_headlines.heading: The LightRAG Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG builds a knowledge graph with LLM extraction, updates it incrementally, and retrieves through dual-level keyword matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG wins LLM-judged comparisons against four baselines on UltraDomain datasets, and uses far fewer retrieval tokens than GraphRAG.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work finds graph-based RAG lacks dynamic updates, and surveys three ways LLMs are combined with graph data.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG is concluded to improve retrieval speed and quality and cut LLM inference costs through graph indexing and incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, a case study against NaiveRAG, and the prompts for graph generation, query generation, keyword extraction and evaluation.

repos.title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
repos.paper_summary:
HALO is a humanoid autonomy system trained on synthetic vision-language-motion data generated across 1,000 procedurally generated homes, with no human teleoperation. Its three onboard layers are a VLM orchestrator that splits free-form requests into subtasks, a motion generator that maps an egocentric RGB image and the active subtask to a 5-second whole-body kinematic plan, and a depth-conditioned tracker trained by distilling privileged PPO experts and then fine-tuning with multi-critic PPO.

On six single skills (go-to, sit, door, crouch, crawl, push), mean success is 91% in 6,000 simulated trials and 91% in 360 real-world trials across six environments not seen in training. Three chained multi-step tasks reach a mean of 69% in simulation and 70% in one real environment. In ablations on sit, training-time continuity conditioning gives 84%, versus 66% with inference-time real-time chunking and 24% without chunking. Removing depth lowers sit to 74%.

Limitations: chained success falls below the product of single-task rates (71% against 89% for Door→Go-To) because the next subtask often begins with its target out of view. The paper suggests adding search and turn-in-place recovery behaviors as a fix.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Humanoid robots need paired vision-language-motion data, which HALO generates in simulation instead of by teleoperation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work relies on scanned rooms, authored templates, or blind trackers; HALO pairs procedural homes with a perceptive tracker.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: A frozen vision-language encoder and a flow-matching decoder generate 5-second motion plans that a depth-conditioned tracker executes.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Single-task success averages 91% in simulation and reality, while chained multi-task success falls to 69% and 70%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Simulation can supply humanoid training data, but task authoring, contact sensing, the generator-tracker interface and orchestration remain limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix details the six-skill corpus, scene generation, baking error, motion filtering, rendering and generator and tracker design.

repos.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
repos.paper_summary: Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting is a zero-shot prompting strategy for large language models that instructs the model to devise a plan dividing a task into subtasks before executing them. The extended variant, PS+, adds instructions to extract relevant variables and calculate intermediate results. On ten datasets covering arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning using GPT-3 (text-davinci-003), PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT by an average of 6.3% on arithmetic tasks, reaching 76.7% accuracy compared to 70.4%. It also exceeds Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought on five of six arithmetic benchmarks. Error analysis on GSM8K shows PS+ reduces calculation errors from 7% to 5% and missing-step errors from 12% to 7%, though semantic misunderstanding errors remain at 27%. The paper notes two limitations: prompt sensitivity requires careful manual design, and the method does not address semantic understanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot chain-of-thought errors are split into calculation, missing-step, and semantic errors, and a plan-based prompt targets two of them.

digest_headlines.heading: Plan-and-Solve Prompting
digest_headlines.headline: Plan-and-Solve prompting uses a zero-shot trigger that asks the model to devise and carry out a plan, followed by an answer-extraction prompt.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use ten benchmarks with text-davinci-003 and compare against zero-shot and few-shot baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT on all arithmetic datasets and averages 76.7 against 77.6 for Manual-CoT.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work places Plan-and-Solve among chain-of-thought methods that use zero-shot prompting and planning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that plan-based zero-shot prompting outperforms Zero-shot-CoT and matches few-shot CoT on some arithmetic datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Prompt design is labour-intensive and the method does not address semantic misunderstanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics
digest_headlines.headline: The paper lists the datasets and their licences and states that the prompts contain no personal information or discriminatory wording.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists trigger-sentence ablations for every dataset and example outputs from Zero-shot-PS+.

repos.title: RobotAgentBench: Towards Open-world Robot Autonomy
repos.paper_summary: RobotAgentBench (RAB) is a simulation benchmark for evaluating robot agents on open-world household tasks. An agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline builds 50 layouts in Isaac Sim, with 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. Tasks test five capabilities: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and disturbance handling. Scenarios test end-to-end progress. Eleven standalone VLA/WAM policies and five agent architectures run on the same 22-dimensional command interface, with 30 instances per task or scenario. The best standalone policy, InternVLA-A1.5, averages 18.0 on task-level scores. The best agent, a code planner and verifier that calls both code and learned policies (C/H/C), averages 48.5 and scores 15.4 on open-ended scenarios, versus 2.0 for the best standalone model there. Recursive self-improvement raises the code-only Codex harness from 31.0 to 42.3 on the task-level average. Limitations: all results are simulated, real-world results are described only qualitatively, and open-ended scores remain low.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current benchmarks test isolated manipulation skills, so this work proposes a benchmark for full robot autonomy in household settings.

digest_headlines.heading: RobotAgentBench
digest_headlines.headline: Real rooms are rebuilt in simulation to create 50 layouts, and five agent architectures are compared under one framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Standalone policies average at most 18.0, while the best agent, a hybrid code and learned-policy design, reaches 48.5.

repos.title: Step-DPO: Step-wise Preference Optimization for Long-chain Reasoning of LLMs
repos.paper_summary:
Step-DPO is a preference optimization method for large language models that treats individual reasoning steps, rather than full answers, as the unit of comparison to improve mathematical reasoning. The method modifies the standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective by conditioning on preceding correct steps and optimizing the probability of the next correct step versus the first erroneous step. This allows the model to pinpoint specific errors in long chains of thought without penalizing earlier correct logic.

The authors construct a dataset of 10K preference pairs using a three-step pipeline: collecting incorrect model outputs, localizing the first error, and sampling self-generated corrections from the reference model. They find that using in-distribution data generated by the model itself yields better results than out-of-distribution data written by humans or GPT-4. On the MATH benchmark, applying Step-DPO to Qwen2-72B-Instruct increases accuracy from 69.4% to 70.8%, while GSM8K accuracy rises from 92.4% to 94.0%. These gains are achieved with fewer than 500 training steps. The approach also improves performance on competition-level problems like AIME 2024, where Qwen2-72B-Instruct scores 4/30 compared to 5/30 for the base instruct model.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Vanilla DPO cannot locate errors in long math reasoning, so Step-DPO compares individual reasoning steps instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods improve math reasoning through prompting, data augmentation or reinforcement learning, but each has stated limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Step-DPO
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO builds preference pairs from the first wrong step, with the model's own correct continuation as the preferred choice.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO raises Qwen2-72B-Instruct to 70.8% on MATH, with approximately a 3% boost for models above 70B.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude Step-DPO with 10K pairs gives significant gains, particularly for large models.

repos.title: LeRobot: An Open-Source Library for End-to-End Robot Learning
repos.paper_summary:
`lerobot` is an open-source Python library for end-to-end robot learning that integrates low-level motor control, data collection, and policy training. It supports eight hardware platforms, including the SO-100 and ALOHA-2, using a shared middleware API for teleoperation. The library introduces `LeRobotDataset`, a standardized format for multimodal robotics data that enables streaming large datasets without full downloads. As of September 2025, the ecosystem includes over 16,000 datasets from 2,200 contributors.

The library provides PyTorch implementations of leading algorithms such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, $\pi_{0}$, and SmolVLA. Inference benchmarks on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 show ACT achieving 5.01 ms latency, while the larger $\pi_{0}$ model requires 209 ms. An asynchronous inference stack decouples action prediction from execution, allowing policies to run on remote machines. Limitations include incomplete coverage of robot embodiments and algorithms, and the lack of low-level optimizations like quantization or graph compilation for practical deployment.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Robot learning tools are fragmented, so the authors present lerobot, an open-source library spanning the full stack from motor control to datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Low-cost open arms cost a fraction of industrial ones, and this accessibility supports decentralized data collection.

digest_headlines.heading: Features
digest_headlines.headline: lerobot supports several low-cost arms, a shared dataset format with 16K+ datasets, and reference implementations of policies.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulation
digest_headlines.headline: Simulation is used only for benchmarking, since the authors find simulation challenging for the contact-rich tasks the library targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: lerobot is presented as a unified open stack, with limits in robot coverage, algorithm count, and inference optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists robot build guides, dataset breakdowns, the streaming dataset design, model and inference examples, and a synchronous versus asynchronous comparison.

repos.title: RAG-Anything: All-in-One RAG Framework
repos.paper_summary: RAG-Anything is a unified multimodal retrieval-augmented generation framework that builds a dual graph over documents: a cross-modal graph anchored on non-text units (figures, tables, equations) and a text-based graph, merged by entity-name alignment. Retrieval combines graph neighborhood expansion with dense embedding search over entities, relations, and chunks, and a VLM answers using text context plus the dereferenced visual content. On DocBench, it reaches 63.4% overall accuracy versus 61.0% for MMGraphRAG, 58.4% for LightRAG, and 51.2% for GPT-4o-mini. On MMLongBench, it reaches 42.8% versus 38.9% for LightRAG and 37.7% for MMGraphRAG. The gap grows with document length: on DocBench it is over 13 points for documents over 100 pages. Ablations on DocBench show 60.0% for chunk-only retrieval and 62.4% without the reranker, against 63.4% for the full system. All baselines use GPT-4o-mini, and accuracy is judged by GPT-4o-mini. The paper reports no variance across runs. Evaluation covers two benchmarks only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems handle only text, so multimodal documents are poorly served; the paper proposes RAG-Anything to fix this.

digest_headlines.heading: The RAG-Anything Framework
digest_headlines.headline: RAG-Anything decomposes documents into typed units, builds two linked graphs, and retrieves through both structure and embeddings.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On MMLongBench, RAG-Anything scores 42.8% overall versus 37.7% for MMGraphRAG, with gains growing on longer documents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work groups graph-enhanced RAG and multimodal RAG, and argues that prior multimodal systems fragment by modality.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that dual-graph retrieval helps long documents and identifies text-centric bias and rigid spatial processing as failure modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, extra case studies, the three multimodal prompts, the accuracy prompt, and failure-case analyses.

repos.title: LlamaFactory: Unified Efficient Fine-Tuning of 100+ Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
LlamaFactory is a unified framework integrating efficient fine-tuning methods to adapt over 100 large language models without custom code. It comprises three modules: a Model Loader attaching adapters like LoRA, QLoRA, and GaLore; a Data Worker standardizing dataset formats; and a Trainer supporting pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, and DPO. A key feature is model-sharing RLHF, which uses dynamic adapter switching to run the full pipeline on a single pre-trained model. The web interface LlamaBoard allows users to configure experiments and monitor training in real time.

The authors validate the framework on an NVIDIA A100 GPU using Gemma-2B, Llama2-7B, and Llama2-13B. On a corpus of roughly 400K tokens from PubMed abstracts, 4-bit QLoRA reduces peak memory to 5.21 GB for Gemma-2B compared to 17.06 GB for full tuning, while LoRA achieves a throughput of 3521 tokens/s. In downstream text generation tasks with 2,000 training examples, LoRA and QLoRA generally match or exceed full-tuning ROUGE scores across eight instruction-tuned models. Limitations include the requirement for adapter-based methods when using quantized weights and the fact that full-tuning Llama2-13B exceeds the 40GB memory limit of the test hardware.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning large language models is costly, so LlamaFactory unifies efficient fine-tuning methods in one framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing fine-tuning frameworks support fewer efficient methods than LlamaFactory, as its feature comparison shows.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques
digest_headlines.headline: The paper groups efficient fine-tuning into optimization methods, such as LoRA, and computation methods, such as flash attention.

digest_headlines.heading: LlamaFactory Framework
digest_headlines.headline: LlamaFactory has three modules, Model Loader, Data Worker and Trainer, with a web interface called LlamaBoard.

digest_headlines.heading: Empirical Study
digest_headlines.headline: Across tested models, quantized low-rank adaptation used the least memory and low-rank adaptation scored best on most generation tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets more modalities, parallel training strategies and stronger methods for conversational models.

digest_headlines.heading: Broader Impact and Responsible Use
digest_headlines.headline: The authors expect the framework to benefit open-source communities, and require users to follow model licenses.

repos.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
repos.paper_summary: SWE-bench is an evaluation benchmark of 2294 software engineering tasks drawn from GitHub issues and their merged pull requests across 12 popular Python repositories. A model receives an issue text and a codebase snapshot and must produce a patch that makes the repository's fail-to-pass tests pass without breaking existing tests. Tasks were collected with a 33-stage pipeline that filters PRs for issue resolution, test changes, and successful execution. The authors also release SWE-bench Lite, a 300-instance subset, a training set (SWE-bench-train, about 19,000 instances from 37 other repositories), and two fine-tuned CodeLlama-Python models, SWE-Llama 7b and 13b, trained with LoRA on attention weights. Context is selected with BM25 retrieval or with oracle files from the reference patch. The best model, Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval, resolves 1.96% of tasks; with oracle retrieval it resolves 4.8%. Performance falls as context length grows. The authors note that the benchmark covers only Python, and that execution-based tests do not capture code efficiency, readability, or comprehensiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks are saturated, so the authors propose SWE-bench, which draws tasks from real GitHub issues.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench pairs GitHub issues with merged pull requests and grades patches by running the repository's tests.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-Llama: Fine-tuning CodeLlama for SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning CodeLlama-Python on issue-patch pairs produces SWE-Llama, open models that edit repositories.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Each model gets context from sparse retrieval or from oracle files that the reference patch edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Claude 2 is the best model at 1.96% resolved, and resolution falls as the total context length grows.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier benchmarks use narrow tasks or single functions, which SWE-bench extends to multi-file repository edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include Python-only tasks, simple baselines, and execution tests that miss readability and efficiency.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench uses public repositories with licenses permitting software use, and involves no human subjects or GitHub user data.

digest_headlines.heading: Reproducibility Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The source code, all 2294 task instances, and technical details for collection and evaluation are provided for reproduction.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers construction, field definitions, execution-based validation, dataset statistics, and case studies of model patches.
